subject: Culture
title: Day of the Dead
description: A 60-second lesson on Day of the Dead.

hook.text: Mexicans build altars for dead relatives, cook their favorite foods, and spend the night in cemeteries.

buildup.text: Día de los Muertos blends Aztec death rituals with Catholic All Saints' Day. Neither tradition alone explains it.

discovery.text: The Aztecs saw death as continuation, not ending. The dead simply moved to another realm and could visit.

twist.text: The holiday was nearly forgotten in northern Mexico. A 20th-century cultural revival brought it back nationwide.

climax.text: Day of the Dead turns grief into celebration. Mourning and joy coexist on the same altar.

punchline.text: The dead come home once a year for dinner.

quiz.question: What two traditions blended to create Día de los Muertos?

details.summary: Mexico's Day of the Dead (November 1-2) honors deceased loved ones with ofrendas, marigolds, sugar skulls, and cemetery picnics. Unlike Western approaches to death, this UNESCO-recognized celebration treats the dead as welcome guests returning for an annual family reunion.
details.whyItMatters: Day of the Dead demonstrates that grief and joy can coexist. Its approach to mortality — communal, colorful, and ongoing — offers a radical alternative to Western death avoidance.
takeaways: Day of the Dead blends pre-Columbian Aztec and Catholic traditions
Marigold petals guide spirits from the cemetery to the home altar
UNESCO recognized it as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2008

faq.question: How is Day of the Dead different from Halloween?
faq.answer: Halloween focuses on fear and disguise. Day of the Dead focuses on love, remembrance, and specific deceased family members. Families build ofrendas with photos, favorite foods, and personal items for their dead. The dead are welcomed, not feared.

faq.question: What are the Aztec roots of Day of the Dead?
faq.answer: The Aztecs held month-long death festivals dedicated to the goddess Mictecacihuatl, Lady of the Dead. Spanish colonizers merged these with All Saints' and All Souls' Days.
